$comment: RF-21 / issue #135: the shared boundary corpus for URL extraction.
chat-service decides which URLs get scanned (scanURLCandidates); the web client
decides which get a clickable anchor (findAutolinks). If the two disagree about
where a URL ends, the client can render a link to an address the safety check
never saw. This file is the single source of expectations that holds them
together: both test suites read it, and both assert the invariant below.
INVARIANT: every href the client produces must appear verbatim among the
candidates the backend extracted from the same input. Under-linking is fine —
the client may produce fewer — but a client href that is not a backend
candidate is a link to something unchecked.
name              what the case is about
input             the message body, exactly as stored
note              why the two differ, when they do
Escapes: invisible and direction-altering characters are written as \uXXXX so
the file stays reviewable and greppable. Every host is under .test or .example,
which are reserved and unroutable — no real address appears here.

cases.name: mixed-case scheme
cases.note: Both sides match the scheme case-insensitively and keep the text verbatim.

cases.name: balanced parentheses
cases.note: The regression this corpus exists for: the backend used to trim the closing paren and scan a different URL from the one the client linked.

cases.name: nested url in query
cases.note: One candidate, not two: the scan consumes the whole run, so the embedded address is never offered as a separate destination.

cases.name: credentials in authority
cases.note: The backend extracts it and its canonicaliser then refuses it as having no consultable reputation. The client refuses to anchor it: an authority section that reads like a hostname is a classic disguise.

cases.name: backslash in authority
cases.note: The parser divergence that matters most. WHATWG normalises the backslash to a slash, making the host evil.test; Go's net/url keeps it in the path, making the host good.test. The client refuses any candidate containing a literal backslash.

cases.name: invalid percent escape
cases.note: Go's url.Parse rejects the escape, so the backend never canonicalises or scans it; WHATWG keeps it verbatim. The client fails closed.

cases.name: percent-encoded parentheses
cases.note: %28/%29 are not brackets to a reader and take no part in the balance, so only the literal wrapping paren is given back.

cases.name: internationalised domain
cases.note: The candidate is the text as written on both sides; punycode conversion happens later, in each side's own resolver.

cases.name: ipv4 literal
cases.note: The backend extracts then refuses IP literals. The client under-links them so WHATWG-normalized legacy spellings cannot navigate to an address different from the scanned string.

cases.name: ipv6 literal
cases.note: The delimiter still keeps the balanced authority, but IP literals are deliberately not anchored.

cases.name: short ipv4 literal
cases.note: WHATWG resolves this historical spelling as 127.0.0.1; Go must refuse it and the client must not anchor it.

cases.name: octal ipv4 literal
cases.note: WHATWG resolves the octal spelling as 127.0.0.1.

cases.name: hex ipv4 literal
cases.note: WHATWG resolves the hexadecimal spelling as 127.0.0.1.

cases.name: protocol relative
cases.note: No scheme, so neither side sees a URL at all.

cases.name: blob wrapping https
cases.note: The backend scans the embedded address, which is the conservative direction for a security check. The client refuses it: a scheme starting inside another token is not a URL the sender wrote.

cases.name: bidi override around a url
cases.note: The scan begins at the scheme, so a leading control is outside the candidate while a trailing one is inside it — the two ends are not symmetric. The client refuses any candidate carrying a direction-altering character at all: the rendered label would not be the resolved address.

cases.name: zero width space inside a url
control character ends the run
cases.note: A C0 control is a terminator on both sides, so the candidate ends before it.

cases.name: scheme inside another token
cases.note: The backend extracts the embedded address and scans it; the client refuses to offer an address the sender did not write.

cases.name: bare mention is not a url
scheme with no host
cases.note: The backend extracts the fragment and its hasHost check then treats it as not-a-link rather than refusing the message. The client will not anchor a URL with no host.
